I have been directed by the board of control to bring to your official notice as the elective representative from this city that, whereas the city of Toronto has made a very considerable investment in respect to harbour and hydro developments, therefore the said city of Toronto does vigorously protest against the passing of any legislation by the government of the Dominion of Canada which would prejudicially affect the ultimate deepening and use of the St. Lawrence river as an oceangoing waterway.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST LOCAL LABOUR ON VANGUARD-MEYRONNE BRANCH
speechtext:
I wish to ask the question of the Acting Minister of Labour. The Canadian Pacific railway are building a branch line from Vanguard to Meyronne, Saskatchewan, in my constituency, and they are receiving some assistance from the $20,000,000 grant from this government. I understand that local men in that district are being discriminated against and that outside men are being brought in, even Americans, who are being hired to work on this railway at from fifty cents to one dollar per day. I would ask the Minister of Labour

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
to have this matter investigated and to see that heads of families who are at present obtaining direct relief from the municipalities receive first consideration, and that the fair wage be paid.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Max D. Cormier for an address to His Excellency the Administrator in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King, and the proposed subamendment of Mr. Gardiner.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Since this debate began
nearly a month ago, there have been a great many developments both inside this house and in the country at large. I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to make a few remarks with regard to the
subamendment which has been proposed from this corner of the house. The particular form which the subamendment has taken represents somewhat of a compromise between the various groups in this corner of the house. We have found that in a great many ways the farmer and labour groups can work in close cooperation, but I must say that in some respects labour would state its case just a little bit differently from the case stated by the farmers-possibly because the needs of the agricultural workers are somewhat different from those of the industrial workers. Had we of the labour group been proposing our own amendment, impossible under the circumstances, we would like to have expressed ourselves somewhat in these terms:
We are of the opinion that there exists in Canada an economic condition that constitutes a national emergency which can be met only by extraordinary measures.
We regret that there is no indication in the speech from the throne of any provision which will adequately meet the pressing needs of hundreds of thousands of industrial workers and agricultural producers.
We believe that present conditions demand the mobilization of our natural resources, technical equipment and financial machinery, to provide a decent livelihood for the people of the Dominion. In our opinion this involves the abandonment of the present wasteful and inefficient competitive system and the adoption of cooperative principles both in our domestic and international relations.
We agree in the forepart of our resolution that in Canada to-day we do face a national emergency. We in the labour group would like to go so far as to say that under those conditions ive should mobilize the entire resources of this country. When the war was on we found it necessary to call upon various industries to contribute. Those in authority introduced conscription. It was felt that the emergency was so great that the entire resources of the country should be mobilized. Finances were forthcoming for the very great effort which the nations of the world had to put forward at that time. Whilst we would not say that the emergency at the present time is so acute as that which prevailed in 1914, we do say that the emergency is great enough to call for the mobilization of all the resources of this country.
I should like to remind the house that the bankers owe their position very largely to special privileges granted by this house. I would like to remind the house that the railway people owe their franchises to special privileges granted by the Dominion of Canada. and so on right along the line, and there seems to be no reason why, when hundreds of thousands of people are on the verge of

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is nasty of them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is the attitude of the communist party towards myself and the group with which I am associated. After the pilgrimage the other day of the group of unemployed led by communists I find this:
The demonstrations of February 25 and April 15 were but dress rehearsals of the demonstrations yet to come. The demonstration of May 1, international labour day will be a continuation of them and will surpass them all.
That article is contained in The Worker of April 18. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is too serious a matter simply to be off by the suggestion which has been made in this house that any man who introduces a question of this kind is promoting riots. I would urge that if the situation is so serious

The Address-Mr. Woodsworlh
that statements may be made in newspapers to the effect that such demonstrations are going to take place in the future it is high time that this parliament discussed the matter. I would point out further that comparatively speaking there are but few communists in this country. But if there is dissatisfaction and if there is want, there is bound to arise a group who will champion the cause of the needy and perhaps play upon the emotions of those who are suffering so much. Passing from Winnipeg to the east-I find in the Montreal Herald this paragraph with regard to the riots that took place last Wednesday in Montreal:
The cops, particularly the plainclothes men, were none too gentle. It was no uncommon sight yesterday afternoon to see some mildeyed and sheep-like appearing pedestrian propelled half way across the road by the toe of a constable's boot. Many times the whack of fist on face resounded through the streets.
Well, I call that .brutal treatment, whether by constituted authority or not, and I would suggest that the way to solve unemployment is not by increasing our police force and encouraging their brutality, but rather by attempting to get at the underlying economic causes.
Let me say that the position even of the communistic group so far has been quite correct. The communists headed the unemployed men in their march to the city halls and there pleaded their case. Further than that they went to the provincial governments-at least they did in my own city of Winnipeg on Wednesday last-begging that something be done for the unemployed. The unemployed have been put off by vague promises ever since last summer. When the elections were being held last July in Winnipeg the municipal authorities were feeding nearly 3,000 people. We were told that the summer would solve the situation. Summer came but there was no marked improvement and all these people have been on the unemployed list day after day, week after week, month after month. During the winter they were told that as soon as spring opened up all the unemployed would be able to find work. It is only a few days ago since I received a letter containing four or five closely written sheets of names of the Swedish unemployed of my home city, asking me if I could not do something to get them jobs on the new Hudson Bay railway or up at Churchill. These Swedish people we all know are among our finest immigrants. They were brought out here under representations that they were to get jobs. They have done good work in the past. Hundreds of them- I am not exaggerating-in my home city alone during the winter were fed at first by their own mission churches, and later by the muni-
{Mr. Woodsvrort.h.]
cipal authorities; now with another summer opening up they do not know what to do. Let me say again that recently at one of the meetings of this Swedish group a communist tried to interfere and break up the proceedings, but he was thrown out. That, however, does not solve the problem of these hundreds of Swedish unemployed, who are among the very best of our citizens. What are we going to do about the matter? We have this situation right across the country.
Yesterday the member for West York (Mr. Lawson) in the course of his speech-a speech for which I have to compliment him; it was a very fine effort indeed, and I think every one was impressed with the wonderful parliamentary ability shown by the hon. gentleman-made one or two statements to which I must take exception. He suggested that we in this corner represented a particular group of people, while he represented all the citizens of his constituency. Now, I do not like that attitude at all so far as I myself am concerned. I take it that since I was elected by a very considerable majority I can very well claim to represent all the citizens of my constituency just as much as he claims to represent every one in West York. At the last election I was not opposed either by the Liberals or the Conservatives, so the two old parties must take their responsibility for having allowed me to come back again. But we of the Labour group do represent a particular group which up to recent years has not had a chance to voice its needs on the floor of this house. And I would urge it is extremely difficult for any one but a lawyer to represent everybody in his constituency. For instance, I have the grain exchange in my constituency, but I do not think any of my farmer friends throughout the west will accuse me of representing the grain exchange and at the same time pleading for the farmers of the prairies. I have also a large number of bankers in my constituency, at least the offices of several of the banks are there, but I do not think the bankers themselves would say that I represent them at the same time as I am representing the needs of the common people of this country.
I have nothing against the bankers individually, they are a decent enough lot of men. but I do say I am not representing the policies of the banks when I come here and plead for the needs of the common people of the west. So I would suggest that this statement of the member for West York is altogether a misleading way of stating the position. I contend that we stand here, not representing this, that and the other interest

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
in our constituency; we represent a certain group that hitherto has been almost without a champion. We come out flatfooted on that point. Again, the member for West York suggests that we "purport" to represent labour, Well, when labour has returned some of us to this house for the past ten years I do not think that that word is in very good taste. Surely we represent labour because the labour men have as much right to be a party as have the farmers or the Liberals or the Conservatives. He suggests that we persist in making inflammatory speeches devoid of practical suggestions. Again, I say that is a purely gratuitous remark to make. I do not think any of us can be successfully charged with making inflammatory speeches; we are simply pointing out the facts in the situation. Further, it cannot be said that we have failed to put forward certain suggestions. If you, Mr. Speaker, will look at the order paper you will find it contains motion after motion, put forward by members of this group; and that has been the case ever since I have been in the house for the past decade. If any suggestions of a practical nature have been put forward, they have come largely from the members in this corner. We have made these suggestions during the present debate, and if I had the time I should be glad to attempt to make them again before I sit down. We have put forward what we regard as practical suggestions. Of course, they are rejected by hon. members on the other side, by the government powers, as being impractical. Well, in that case I suggest that it is distinctly the part of the government to make suggestions. In fact I think we are all sufficiently familiar with parliamentary procedure and British traditions to recognize that fundamentally it is the government that is responsible for policies. It is our part to show the need for certain legislation; it is the government's to work out the policies. If the government wants suggestions, right in our subamendment will be found a few practical suggestions, and it is for the government now to say whether it will accept these in the spirit in which they are proffered or whether it will arrogantly brush them aside and say that in its own way it will solve the problems now confronting the country.
The member for West York states that all he wants for the working people of the Dominion is the maintenance of the system of collective bargaining. Let me say to him that to-day there are very few workers who are allowed to bargain collectively. The vast majority of our working people are outside the trade unions altogether, and when they
are members of such unions they usually have to go on strike in order to maintain the principle of collective bargaining. The hon. member for West York says all he wants is the maintenance of a family life and fairly high standard of living. That is all we want, but those standards do not exist to-day. You have only to turn to the official records of the Department of Labour to find that statement amply corroborated; you have only to refer to the evidence given before our committee on industrial and international relations to find ample corroboration, and you have onlj' to turn to the pages of Hansard for the last few weeks to find how much below those standards our people are at the present time. That kind of thing is simply an attempt to divert public attention from the real issue.
I noticed that the hon. member for West York, posed-I was about to say-but since I objected to his use of a word of that kind I will withdraw that word and put it this way. His name appears on the letterhead of the Canadian Workers' Association as legal adviser. I hold in my hand a communication from the secretary of that organization stating that their association is running a series of three mass meetings in the interests of un-t employment insurance. The first of these meetings will be held on a certain date, and one of our group is asked to be present. I would suggest that this question of unemployment insurance is one of the things we have been bringing forward year after year, and it is on the order paper again this year in the name of my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). If the hon. member for West York is really serious in his interest in the working people I would urge that he use his influence with the Prime Minister to see that there is enacted at this session of parliament a measure of unemployment insurance. The hon. member for West York, unfortunately, in having a fling at labour is really more or less following in the lead of the Prime Minister himself. The Prime Minister said the other day:
No good service is being done to the country by the exaggerations made by some of those who have addressed the chamber this afternoon.
I object to that form of statement. I do not know whether the Prime Minister was referring to me, whether he was referring to my colleague or whether he was referring to some of the farmer members who had spoken. It seems to me that if we have exaggerated or if we have misstated the case it ought to be clearly understood what man has made the exaggeration or the misstatement, and then

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
we would be in a position to answer. The Prime Minister then went on to discuss the academic question as to whether the rich man should put his money in the bank or should spend it lavishly. The Prime Minister was rather of the opinion, I gathered, that it would be better to spend his money lavishly than to put it in the bank. I always imagined that he had such a high regard for the banks that he would have thought that putting it into the banks would be the surest way to put it into the channels of industry.
The Prime Minister suggests that the rich man should spend his money lavishly. Our contention in this house is altogether aside from that. Really we are not very particular as to whether the rich man saves or spends. What we are trying to say is that to-day, under the existing conditions, no man has a right to millions and no corporation has a right to the power which millions give. It is not with us the particular question as to how this or that man spends his wealth; the point is that wealth comes to-day because of the social privileges which are being given by governmental authority, and if there are those to whom wealth comes almost automatically while there are those who have so little of it that they are on the streets to-day, our contention is that there should be a readjustment in our regulations, in our forms of administration and in our laws themselves so that there may be a more equitable distribution of that wealth, which I think every thoughtful man will concede is produced not through the efforts of any individual or any particular group of individuals but which is produced as the result of the efforts of thousands and tens of thousands of people working to-day, as we work, collectively.
That is the position we take, and that is the situation to which I would like to direct the attention of the house. The other day my good friend the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) undertook to question some of my statements. He was good enough to say that he did not think I would mislead the house, because he said I had been the minister in a church years ago which he had attended. I am very thankful to him for the very great kindness that underlay his statement and which has persisted during the last twenty-five or thirty years, but when he proceeds to make this statement I feel that I must take exception to it. Referring to myself, he asked:
Why is he bringing in these things and knocking down the price of lands?
That, Mr. Speaker, is the kind of statement which I think should be challenged. I recall

twenty-five years ago, when I was connected with the church, when a man told me that I ought not to talk about certain things because I was "knocking" the price of real estate. At that time I was living down in the northern part of my city of Winnipeg among the foreign born, and an epidemic was sweeping the country that summer, a child's disease, of which nearly 200 children in my district died within a fortnight. They were dying in North Winnipeg almost three times as quickly as they were dying in the other parts of the city which had better opportunities for caring for the children, and when I put this statement in a diagram and wanted to show it at a public health exhibition which was then being presented in my city-and this was twenty-five years ago-one gentleman belonging to the real estate board objected and said, "Oh, no, you must not exhibit that chart. It would knock real estate."
I had one of my own children lying ill at that time, Mr. Speaker. We had a good doctor and good nurses; the child had good care and we pulled the little chap through. The children of my neighbours, however, were dying by the score, and I remember one day being called to conduct a funeral service over the body of one of these children. We went out to the grave side; there were twenty little fresh made graves all in a row. There was the grave into which we were to lower the tiny body, and behind that were half a dozen graves half dug. The children were not dead yet, but the grave diggers were getting ahead with their work. I was supposed to read the funeral service so familiar to many of us here; "For as much as it has pleased Almighty God, in his wise providence to take out of the world the soul of the deceased." I said in my heart, "That is not true." I knew the reasons for the death of those children. Those reasons were bad milk, bad housing and bad social arrangements, and I was not going to blame any God with being responsible for it.
That was one of the big events in my life, Mr. Speaker, and when I was blamed for trying to get better health conditions, and when they said it would knock the price of real estate, the situation presented itself to me in this way: if it was my duty to read the funeral service over the body of a dead child it was much more my duty to save the children then living. I would urge upon this house that the welfare of the men, the women and the children of this country is worth much more than the price of real estate in the constituency of Marquette. I know my hon. friend does not really believe the contrary; he did not think of the implications. I would not

The Address-Mr. Coote
dare to say that he was hardhearted; the hon. members of this house are not hardhearted but they do not realize the conditions which prevail in many parts of this country.
When the unemployed interviewed the Premier of Manitoba at Winnipeg the other day he called their attention to the fact that that province had passed a resolution about a year ago urging the Dominion government to call a Dominion-provincial conference to which all provinces would send representatives to consider the advisability of amending the British North America Act so that the Dominion government could establish a Dominion-wide system of unemployment insurance. This is what we are urging upon the government. I find that requests of this sort are beginning to come in from other parts of Canada, even from eastern Canada. Only to-day I received in my mail a resolution passed by the township of East York, to this effect:
.... realizing the appalling situation existing in the township of East York and throughout this country in general through unemployment. and further realizing that unemployment is getting beyond the control of the local municipalities,
We hereby demand that the federal government pass legislation as soon as possible to bring into force unemployment insurance, on the same principle as exists in Great Britain.
I do not believe the ratepayers of East York are communists even though they use the words "we demand."
I have received many letters from many parts of the country. These letters are sent to me particularly because I represent a distinct labour group in this house, and because I have spoken on unemployment. As all hon. members know, when one speaks on any subject of general interest many people send him letters and resolutions. The following was received from Calgary-I select this one because that is the city of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). It reads:
Yesterday the Calgary employment bureau here had registered 2,848 men for whom no work was available. This number will shortly be augmented by the closing of the relief camps. Housewives report that increasing numbers of men are asking for food at their doors. Private citizens are continually giving meal tickets and orders for beds, as well as cash donations, to unemployed men. Small grocers and rooming house keepers are burdened through extending credit to men on part time relief work or without work. We feel it would be fairer to the citizens and better for the men who are unemployed if they could be supported by relief or relief work of which the cost is borne by all taxpayers.
I will not take the time of the house to refer to other resolutions, but these are typical 22110-49
examples. A despatch, dated April 9, from Sudbury, to the Toronto Star, reads as follows:
Sudbury's unemployed has reached 3,438, of which '450 are married men with families. The soup kitchen is still serving an average of 450 meals a day. The city is also supplying 170 families with bread, clothing and fuel.
. The papers are full of such stories. Only yesterday I noticed the following in the press as coming from Sturgeon Falls:
A pathetic climax to the period of destitution which has left many citizens of this northern community starving and ragged was enacted yesterday afternoon at the little town hall when a band of citizens, men and women, asked permission to send their children barefooted to school.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to take up a few minutes' time to bring to the attention of the government a matter which I would have brought up on the orders of the day were it possibe to get satisfaction at that time. I refer particularly to the conditions existing in one of the towns iu the coal district of the Crowsnest pass, and I do not think I could do better than to read a letter which I received from the secretary of the Mine Workers' Union. This letter is sent from Bellevue, dated April 8, 1931, and reads:
I was instructed to write you and let you know of the conditions in Bellevue at the present time. The mine at Bellevue is only working one or two days per week and lias only worked twenty-two days for the three months of the present year.
We have now about forty men laid off and taking the manager at Bellevue at his word, there will be 180 men laid off by the 15th of April. Blairmore will no doubt be in the same position as we are.
At our regular meeting last Sunday we passed a motion to the effect that we are in favour of everyone getting a share of the work that is going with no men laid off. This motion was passed unanimously with around 120 present.
I would draw the attention of the house to the following sentence:
It was the general opinion of the members present that if we must starve then let us all starve together.
Our committee will meet the general manager on Friday and in the event of the manager failing to comply with our request for a fair share-up of the work, I will immediately write you.
I have another letter from the same man, dated April 16, which reads:
About a week ago I wrote you in regard to the awful conditions that prevail in the mining camp at Bellevue. As I stated in my lass letter to you I would write you as soon as we had our interview with Mr. Yissac.

The Address-Mr. Coote
We passed a motion at our last regular meeting which was passed unanimously by a well attended meeting. Our motion was to the effect that we want a fair share-up of the work that is to be had with no men laid off.
O.ur committee met Mr. Vissac on the morning of the 14th April and the general manager of the West Canadian Collieries made it plain to us that there would be 100 men laid off and in the near future, if things do not pick up then there will be some more men laid off. The same number of men will be laid off at Blairmore.
Our proposition which you yourselt must admit is very fair was turned down by Mr. Yissac and we feel that the general manager's attitude is anything but fair.	.
You must readily understand if this laying-off of men is carried through it is going to cause much trouble in the Pass as no doubt the other companies will follow the lead of Mr. Vissac.	.
It seems that the mines here are not being operated in the best interests of either the worker or the country and we appeal to you to intervene on our behalf and use all the influence you have to get for us the very fair proposition we put to our general manager Vissac. To throw a few hundred men on an already overstocked unemployment market at the present time appears to be very bad policy.
This letter is signed by the secretary of the Bellevue Miners' Union.
As there is no Minister of Labour in the house I would appeal to the hon. Minister of Mines (Mr. Gordon) to take this matter up and endeavour to arrive at a satisfactory solution. I would again draw the attention of the house to the words, "It was the general opinion of the members present that if we must starve then let us all starve together." I do not think that resolution exaggerates the true condition of affairs. These men worked only 126 days last year. Some of the outside men draw only $4.40 per day and hon. members who are good at mental arithmetic can figure out just how far that will go towards providing the decent standard of living to which the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) referred yesterday as being a desirable condition for Canada. These men and their families are in absolute want. I know of one case where a man had $3,000 in the Home bank when it failed and he still has $1,500 coming to him in theory. He is forced to draw relief in order to keep from starvation, his family consisting of a wife and six children. He was a very thrifty man and he did the best he could, but he is forced to draw relief from the town of Blairmore.
The condition at Bellevue is particularly serious. This is a small community and I am sure there is no possibility of relief, either direct or indirect, being given to the miners out of the $20,000,000 voted for unemployment re-

lief as the town of Bellevue would be unable to pay their share of the expenditure necessary. No wonder the secretary of the Miners' Union says that if all these men are laid off, there will be trouble. There are five big mines in this area. If the other five mines follow the same policy that has been inaugurated at Bellevue, it means that about 1,000 men will be laid off within the next week or two. What are these 1,000 men to do? This mining area is located in the mountains; there is no farming country around it where these people can go, and they have not the money to move out in any ease. I have examined the pay slips of some of the miners at Bellevue; I have noted one case where a man worked every day the mine was open during the months of January and February, and for those two months he averaged $26.65 per month. Those are the net wages he received. He endeavoured to keep himself, bis wife and four children on that. Now the proposal of the management is to lay off a large number of these men and to divide up the work amongst the men whom they retain on the pay-roll. I again ask the government to send a man from the Department of Labour into that camp to try to arrange a satisfactory solution of the difficulty between the company and the men. If those men have to he laid off, this should not be done until some provision is made for them and their families when that lay-off occurs, because the day their names are removed from the pay list, (that day their credit will be stopped at the stores. What, then, are they going to live on? The community cannot give them direct relief and it will be a crime if this action is allowed to be taken by the management unless some provision is made to take care of them.
May I say that I am glad the subamendment has been moved by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner). I could not honestly vote for the motion. I took the trouble this morning to look up the motion, the words of which are rather striking. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Cormier) moved:
That a humble address be presented to His Excellency the Administrator of Canada, to thank His Excellency for the gracious speech which he has been pleased to make to both houses of parliament, at the opening of this session.
Those are very grateful and humble words. I thought: What is in the speech from the throne that we should be so very grateful for? I read over the speech from the throne and I could find in it very little to make me really thankful. Of course in this case His Excel-

The Address-Mr. Young
lency means the Prime Minister and it does not seem possible that the speech from the throne could have been written by the same man who delivered such eloquent speeches during the election campaign. If this speech from the throne were in line with the speech, for instance, delivered at Winnipeg with which the campaign was opened, we might thank His Excellency for it. I have in my hand a clipping taken from a United States publication reading:
The contrast between the Republican campaign assurances and the present reality is pretty vivid.
By the change of one word that fits the case here very nicely. Then it would read:
The contrast between Conservative campaign assurances and the present reality is pretty vivid.
I can find no reason why I should vote for the motion for the address. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) does not suit me very well; it is entirely negative in character, and at a time as serious as this we certainly require some very constructive proposals. I am pleased that the subamendment has been moved, because it suggests something constructive to the house. It contains three very definite proposals : the appointment of a committee to examine into the causes and extent of the present depression and to suggest action to relieve present suffering, correct the present situation and render less probable the recurrence of such disasters in the future. That is surely a worthy suggestion to make to the house. Already in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne some suggestions have been made, and I think they should be considered by this committee. This is surely so reasonable that the government will accept it.
The second suggestion which we make is federal action to secure the granting of sufficient credit to enable the western farmers to put in their crops. The government must be convinced of the necessity for that. Speeches delivered by some of their own supporters from western Canada should be quite ample to convince them in that regard.
I want to read just one paragraph from a letter which I hold in my hand, because I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the house. This is a letter which I received this morning from a very reliable gentleman in my constituency. He says:
We have been encouraged in the use of credit and the present is no time for its withdrawal. The banks have almost closed down entirely on credit and farmers who have turned over to tractors are finding it almost impossible to finance seeding operations.
I cannot refrain from reading the last paragraph of the letter, because it deals with the question of unemployment which we have emphasized in our subamendment.
It looks to me as though the situation was getting worse, unemployment increasing, wages coming down and no opening at all for those completing their educational training and looking for positions. I believe the situation is worse in this class than any other. Numbers of trained boys coming on and large numbers being let out of salaried positions every day. The Canadian Pacific Railway has let most of their employees out here, men with years of training and service. Speak of communism and socialism as you will, at least it oan show nothing worse than the present situation in capitalistic countries.
I do not think I can do better than close with that quotation. Surely in the face of the conditions which have been so fully set before the house, the government should be willing to accept the subamendment which has been moved from this corner.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is a matter for regret that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the government assume the attitude they do towards questions directed to them on the orders of the day. If information is asked for in the house, especially at a time like this, it is in the interest of the government to furnish it as far as possible. Though I cannot agree with the Prime Minister in any of his policies, I have a certain personal regard for him, and I do not like to see him adopting in this chamber a practice that will tend more and more to shake the confidence of the people in his sincerity and integrity.
This afternoon I tried to ask him a question and I endeavoured to lay a foundation to explain what the question would involve in order that he might intelligently comprehend and answer it, but I was denied the privilege so I shall take this opportunity of explaining to the house exactly what I had in mind. In a portion of my constituency there is a considerable stretch of what we call heavy land. It is very productive land, level, of uniform quality and texture, and it lends itself to tractor farming. Practically all the farmers on this land have gone in for tractor farming, many of them having entirely done away with their horses. Economic conditions of late have made it necessary for those farmers to look closely at every cent which they have to pay out. They must cut costs wherever possible, and they find that the price which they have to pay for gasoline is seven cents higher than the wholesale price. On the 6th April of this year, the farmers of one of those districts held a meeting at the village of Riceton and formed a cooperative
The Address-Mr. Young

association to buy their own gasoline. They figured that by so doing they could save five of the seven cent spread between the wholesale and the retail prices. I did not intend to read as much of this letter as I am going to read now, but as I have time I shall read a little more of it to let the house appreciate exactly what was in the minds of these farmers. The letter reads:
We had an interesting meeting Saturday night at Riceton comprising farmers over a large area (most of Lajord municipality) and formed an association chiefly to purchase gasoline.
This is a big question. There is now apparently seven cent spread between wholesale and retail in this district and we can probably get back about five cents in patronage dividends and I have been prodding our boys in Saskatchewan house re gas price during session but little has been done. Mr. Stewart gave notice of a bill but withdrew the bill. I understand from Dr. Urich that the reason given was an agreement with the Dominion government. I asked Mr. Patterson (Milestone) Saturday night about it and he practically admitted that the oil companies bluffed the government out of it and that the government learned that the price would probably go up instead ot down if an investigation was started into prices.
These farmers formed a co-operative organization to buy their own gasoline. They were iocated in the village of Riceton, where there were three storage plants for gasoline owned by three different private oil .companies. The farmers went to one company and said, "We will buy your plant if you care to sell it, and if you do not, we will build another one." So the company decided to sell their plant to the farmers and the following letter, of which I shall read a part, is the sequel to that deal. It is written by Mr. W. S. Kirkpatrick, managing director of the Puritan Oil Company Limited, which is the company that sold its plant to the farmers. It is dated Regina, April 14, 1931, and reads in part as follows:
On April 10th we disposed of one of our bulk plants, located .at Riceton, Saskatchewan to the Riceton Co-operative Association, an association membership composed of farmers throughout that district. At Riceton in addition to our former plant there were also the Imperial and B. A. located at this point w'ith bulk storage. On Saturady morning I interviewed the manager of the Imperial Oil Company in regard to shipping a carload of gasoline to this Association at Riceton. Their manager apparently was very much put out with the thought that this association was formed at that particular point. I might state had we not sold our plant to them, it was their intention to erect a fourth set of tanks, and there -was no business in that particular community _ for four sets of tanks, in fact there is not sufficient for three.
At the time of ordering this car their manager informed me that it would be impossible to

get a shipment out on prompt shipment as they were some forty tank ears behind in shipping. In less than five minutes, without any further information he increased this to fifty cars back ordered. A few moments later he called the refinery superintendent on the phone and while he did not repeat any figures which were given him by the refinery superintendent, the amount was increased to seventy-five cars back ordered, and that he did not know when a shipment could be made, although they were desirous of the business. The writer called him this morning to see if the shipment had actually been made as yet, and he informed me that it had not and did not know when it could be made on account of the shortage of cars and back orders.
I got in my car this morning and drove by their plant to see how many cars actually -were available, as we are very positive it was nothing but a stall to keep these people from receiving gasoline. I found in actual count the following on trackage west of the refinery, 38 empty tank cars stored. Sixteen of them were Imperial Marvelube red cars and green cars, the balance T.C.L.X. Quite a few of the T.C.L.X. cars I might state are used for the Imperial and B. A. shipping. I then drove to the back of the refinery loading rack, and counted 22 cars stored back there. I might state it was impossible to see all the cars that were stored on account of tankage, but would judge there were possibly six or eight that were not visible.
We might also state that the refinery at Regina on account of storage being full and their country storage being full have been laying off men continuously and are only operating the refinery on a skeleton crew endeavouring to reduce their stocks previous to operating on full capacity.	. .	.
We are absolutely positive that this is simply a stall to keep this co-operative association from having supplies, and thought at this time this information might be valuable to the organization.
There is a postscript which reads as follows:
P.S.-This morning we offered to furnish the Imperial Oil an empty tank car if they were still short to handle this shipment, and their local manager refused to accept this offer.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the situation. The Imperial Oil Company at Regina, having the only refinery in Saskatchewan, have deliberately set out to deny to the people of that country the right to buy oil or gas from anyone except themselves and at their own prices. When the farmers undertook to form a cooperative association to buy their own oil and gas, this company refused to furnish them with gasoline on the pretext that it had no cars, when about eighty empty tank cars were standing on their siding. I asked the minister a few moments ago if he would remove the duty on gasoline to allow the farmers to bring it in from the United States free of duty. If he will not, I would ask the government to make an investigation into

The Address-Mr. Neill
this case and to see to it that effective measures are taken to compel the Canadian oil refineries to furnish gasoline to whomsoever wants to buy it and has the money to pay for it. That is the least which the government can do in view of what it has done to increase the price of gasoline and other articles to the farmer.

speechtext:
Now that my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) has introduced the question of the gasoline tax I would like to mention a condition that obtains in the west. At the session last September a duty of 2| cents was imposed on gasoline, which previously came in free. I protested at the time and suggested to the government that they should allow the same exemption as obtains in the province. The province imposes a tax of 5 cents a gallon on gasoline, but exempts farmers and fishermen from paying the tax when the gasoline is used in their operations, and machinery is provided by which they can get a rebate. But the government last September imposed a tax of 2J cents and made it apply on gasoline used by fishermen. They also made a change in the customs tariff and in the Customs Act, and it is in connection with the operation of the latter act, I fancy, that the trouble of which I now wish to speak has arisen more particularly. The fishermen on the west coast engaged in trolling compete with the United States fishermen in the open ocean beyond the three-mile limit, where, of course, the ocean is as open to the American fishermen as it is to our Canadian fishermen, but the market for the class of fish which our Canadian fishermen on the west coast catch at this season of the year is almost entirely in the United States. The United States has a duty of 2 cents a pound on fish entering that country shipped by Canadians. That alone gives the American fisherman an enormous advantage over his Canadian competitor. If we are going to increase that handicap by a tax on gasoline-the Canadian fisherman has to pay 24 cents a gallon for the class of gasoline he uses in his little fishing boat as compared with 8 cents a gallon-the Imperial gallon in both cases-which the American fisherman pays in Seattle-it will be readily understood what a great handicap is imposed on our citizen fishermen. I am told by those in a position to know that the cost of gasoline amounts to from 30 to 35 per cent of the operating costs, so it can be seen at a glance under what a serious handicap our Canadian fishermen operate.
It is not so much that American gasoline is being dumped into this country. It is not being dumped. It is being offered for sale in Canada at the same price as it is offered for sale in the United States, but the customs officials out there are now seeking to impose the dumping duty, not on its merits as we know the dumping duty, but in a roundabout way. To be applied on its merits the dumping duty must be applied to an article which is sold in Canada cheaper than in the country of origin. But the customs officials are seeking to impose it by way of a fictitious condition which they create by resorting to subsection 2, I think it is, of section 36 of the Customs Act, under which they say that the value for duty purposes-I am quoting the act from memory-shall in no case be less than the cost of production in the country of origin, plus a fair profit, plus freight. In that way they will be entitled to fix the value so as to allow the dumping duty to be put on and bring the cost of the American gasoline up from 8 cents to 24 cents a gallon. I would ask the minister in charge of this matter, when he is taking steps to guarantee cost of production plus a reasonable profit, whatever that may be, plus the cost of freight for the American manufacturer of gasoline, would it not be better first to guarantee to our Canadian fishermen the cost of production plus a reasonable profit, plus freight to where his product is sold. It is going to make enormous and untenable difficulties for our Canadian fishermen and I would suggest that in this particular matter the provisions of section 36 of subsection 2 might be waived or at least ignored.

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question? The question is on the subamendment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before the
amendment to the amendment is put, Mr Speaker, I should like to say a word with reference to its nature and to what has been said of it by way of comparison with the original amendment moved by myself.
The amendment of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), which, as has been said this afternoon, represents the collective thought of the independent group in this house, is in the nature of an addition and expansion of my amendment. It is in no sense contradictory of it. It in fact corroborates the representations of the amendment. The subamendment is more comprehensive; it is more suitable as an
774	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
addition to the amendment I have moved than as a substitution for it. Had I been moving my amendment at this stage of the debate I would probably have made it more comprehensive. The subamendment, it is true, as it stands is an alternative to the amendment I have moved. I am prepared to admit that as an alternative in certain of its features there is much to commend it. I believe hon. gentlemen at the far end of this chamber equally believe that my amendment has also very much to commend it.
When I moved the original amendment the house had before it only the speech from the throne. In that speech there were indications that in the course of time the house would be favoured with some concrete evidences of the intentions of the government to meet existing conditions which, according to the speech itself, were regarded as exceptional and serious. For example the speech from the throne contained the following words:
It will be your privilege to consider certain measures designed by my ministers to ameliorate existing conditions-
Also the following:
My ministers are aware that changing conditions in the world's markets may necessitate further intervention by my government, which is prepared to render whatever additional assistance may be deemed advisable in the national interest.
The presence of this statement in the speech from the throne would indicate that to meet the existing situation, the government had had in mind the enactment of additional measures.
It is usual, Mr. Speaker, in a debate which lasts for a considerable period of time and in the course of which the administration is questioned with respect to proposed legislation that some member of the ministry on behalf of the government gives to parliament at least an intimation of what may be expected. Although this debate has run on for more than five weeks we have had from the ministry in that length of time no expression whatever of its intention in regard to legislation of any kind to meet existing conditions which admittedly are of a most serious nature. The two features which have been stressed by all hon. members who have spoken on this side of the house, regardless of the group or party to which they may belong, were first the seriousness of the agricultural distress and secondly the extent and seriousness of unemployment in urban centres. With regard to these all important matters

hon. gentlemen opposite have sat as dumb as oysters. We have had no expression whatever from the ministry as to what they intend doing to meet existing difficulties.
May I mention a further circumstance. We are differently situated with respect to this debate on the speech from the throne than we have been in respect of others which have taken place in parliament. Owing to the lateness at which the session was called there have been on two or three occasions motions to suspend the rules of the house in order that the ministry might proceed a stage further with necessary business. Such action was essential in order to vote the salaries of civil employees. The estimates for the present fiscal year were placed upon the table of the house and are now before us. Ordinarily they would not have been available to hon. members until after the completion of the debate on the speech from the throne. However they are now in our possession and we have had an opportunity to peruse them. I venture to say there is not an hon. member of the house who can point to a single proposed expenditure which in any way is intended expressly to meet either the acute agricultural distress or the unfortunate situation existing with regard to unemployment. That very materially alters the position from what it was at the time I proposed the amendment which appears in my name. Hon, gentlemen in the far corner of the house have had the benefit of a discussion stressing immediate needs which has lasted over five weeks. They have knowledge of two very important facts, one positive in its nature, the other negative which I had not at the time I moved my amendment. The first of these is the positive evidence as shown by the estimates that no special provision is being made to meet agricultural distress in the rural districts or the extensive unemployment in the cities and towns. Evidence of the same thing, negative perhaps in its character, is to be found in the complete silence of the ministry, notwithstanding the representations which from time to time have been made to them during this debate. For those reasons I feel that hon. members in the far corner of the house are at this stage entirely right when they come forward with a subamendment which urges upon the administration immediate action in regard to those two all important phases of our national economic life.
I wish to direct a further remark particularly to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
Owing to the serious conditions of the country at the present time, I think he owed it to the people's representatives in parliament to have been present in this house, and to have listened to the speeches which have been made during the course of this debate. I know he has many onerous duties to perform which of necessity demand much of his time. As Prime Minister of Canada and as leader of the House of Commons his place while the house is in session is in parliament. Had he chosen to absent himself occasionally during or for an afternoon or evening, I would not have raised my voice in criticism, but I venture to say that with the exception of listening to me, during my very long speech, he did not extend a similar courtesy to a single lion, member on this side of the house. It is true he was in his seat while one or two of his own members spoke, but those instances were few indeed. The right hon. gentleman invariably chose to leave his seat immediately following the order to proceed with this debate, and throughout the whole of the five weeks and more he has been in the house for only a very short time. If he had remained here I have no doubt he would have been very much impressed by what has been said by hon. members on this side of the house as to the need of immediate attention and the need of going with greater care into the causes contributing to existing conditions.
Not only has the Prime Minister paid no attention to the debate but his ministers likewise have contributed nothing in the way of an expression of view on the part of the government, and nothing to indicate its attitude. It is true the house was favoured by a contribution to the debate from the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), but there was not a word in the speeches they delivered with reference to government policy. Notwithstanding the fact that on the treasury benches are many hon. gentlemen who have had wide parliamentary experience, we have not heard in the course of this debate a single word from one of them. I affirm, Mr. Speaker, that in this attitude the government is not carrying on the business of the country in a parliamentary way. It is not fulfilling its function as a government when, in a debate as important as this one, no member of the administration has chosen to make or been permitted to make a single contribution with respect to the all-importanit matters under discussion. I am forced to the conclusion that in the matter of its own views
the ministry feels insecure; it must feel that its policies are not as mature as they should be. It would certainly appear that there is need for something in the nature of counsel and advice to be secured perhaps by further investigation. Holding that view, I confess to a very real sympathy with the major proposal of the subamendment which has been moved and which suggests that:
Your Excellency's advisers should give consideration to the appointment of a special committee of parliament, to which committee would be assigned the duty of examining into the causes and extent of the present depression.
That is very moderately and very carefully worded. It places nothing in the way of compulsion upon the administration. It is a mere suggestion that the ministry give consideration to the appointing of a parliamentary committee. I agree with one hon. member who spoke this afternoon in his view as to the limitations of parliamentary committees to achieve anything in a short time; but in a situation such as now exists I certainly think that a committee, which would have upon it members of all parties in this house, and would have the privilege of bringing before it representative individuals from all parts of the country, might do very much in the way of bringing about that cooperative spirit which has been referred to as being so desirable between all parties in the house at a time such as the present and with respect to a great public emergency such as is to be found in more than one phase of the existing economic depression. With that part of the subamendment, I feel myself in entire accord.
The subamendment continues with respect to what is desirable in the interval, between the appointing of a committee and its findings and makes in this connection two concrete suggestions. One is that the administration should give consideration to some scheme of federal assistance to the farmers with respect to their spring operations. When I first heard that clause being discussed I felt it might be taken as a reflection upon the banks that in some way they had failed to discharge their full duty. From a perusal of the clause, however, I do not think that such could Have been the intention and such is certainly not its meaning. The wording as a matter of fact makes it clear that the situation is such that the banks would not be doing their duty were they to attempt to make certain loans in the existing circumstances. At least it seems to me that the clause is capable of that interpretation. It reads:
(a) That the failure or inability of our banks to provide the credit which is essential to our
770	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
farmers in respect to their spring operations, render it imperative that consideration be given to some system of federal assistance, whether directly, by way of bank guarantee, or otherwise.
The member far Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) will correct me if I am wrong, but I take this to mean that the banks find conditions in the farming areas throughout western Canada are such that they would not be, justified in making loans on the security which they are able to obtain. That being the case, and this being spring, and spring operations being impeded through the dire necessity of many of those in the rural parts of the country, the subamendment suggests that the federal government should consider some form of ascist-ance to meet the emergency. My recollection is that over and over again the government has at times of distress given substantial assistance to farmers in connection with their seeding and other agricultural operations; and if there ever was a time when something of the sort would seem to be necessary, that time it would seem is the present.
The other clause of the subamendment is:
(b) That the serious situation which still prevails in respect of unemployment demands that consideration be given to some immediate action looking toward increased employment, and a further measure of direct relief where such is found necessary.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the necessity of some such step must appeal to every hon. member. The need for immediate assistance being granted to meet the existing situation of unemployment has been made more obvious than ever, and the ministry, if it agrees to that particular request, will only be carrving out what at one time or another it has stated was its policy.
In these circumstances I feel that I should like to support the subamendment, and I intend to do so. If the subamendment carries, a special committee will be appointed which will go into all phases of the present ind is-trial situation. That special committee will not proceed very far in its investigation before it will discover the truth of what is alleged in the amendment I have moved. The amendment which I moved some five we-.ks ago expresses the opinion that if certain proposals-
-and certain other of the policies of the government are persisted in, as wTould appear to be the intention of the government as outlined in the speech from the throne, the very serious condition which exists at the present time will be intensified rather than relieved.
I believe it to be true that every hon. member on this side of the house who has spoken, no matter to which group or party he belongs, has given expression to the view

that the tariff increases made at the special session have tended to make conditions in Canada worse rather than better. If a policy of further tariff increase is going to be persisted in, we may look for the economic condition of this country being made even more difficult then it is at present.
Just this word in conclusion. In reference to the amendment which I have moved certain hon. members have said that it is largely negative in character. They have so characterized it because in their view it does not propose some concrete measure such as they have proposed in their subamendment. May I say that what is preventive in its nature may be much more positive in character than anything that may be remedial. The measures which hon. members in the far corner are suggesting are largely remedial in character. If there had been preventive measures adopted at the outset then there might not be any necessity for the remedial legislation they are seeking at the present time. We have before us a clear demonstration of legislation which was enacted at the special session working a positive injury to the agricultural and indeed to other interests in this country. My amendment states that to persist in that policy, as the speech from the throne implies the government intends to do, will only serve to make matters worse. I submit that I am making a positive, not a negative contribution to the relief of the existing situation when I ask this house to declare that the government should discontinue a policy which has already proven inimical to the best interests of the country. If the subamendment does carry, we will have the opportunity for a fuller discussion. If it does not carry, I hope the amendment which I have moved, and which is in the nature of an alternative, will receive substantial support, and that between the two we shall get from hon. gentlemen opposite at least something in the nature of definite action.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, -most hon. members of
this chamber have seen exhibitions of vacillation on more than one occasion by the right hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Mackenzie King), but he has never done himself quite as much justice as he has to-day. He has never made it more clearly apparent to the people of this country than he has this afternoon, that he has no fixed opinions beyond getting a few votes to support any amendment that may be in opposition to the government.
Behold the spectacle. On the 16th day of March, 1931, the right hon. gentleman moved,

The Address-Mr. Bennett
as an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, an amendment reading as follows:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that this house, while recognizing the serious economic conditions prevailing throughout the world, regrets that the policies of His Majesty s government have not only failed to afford a remedy for employment and agricultural distress, as pledged by the Prime Minister and his colleagues, but have served further to prejudice the deplorable position of the agricultural interests, thereby causing additional unemployment and substantially reducing the national revenue.
The house believes that the proposals made to the Imperial economic conference and the manner in which they were submitted and discussed by the Prime Minister of Canada were responsible for the failure of the conference to accomplish its purpose in London, and that the successful development of Canada's trade relations with Great Britain has been adversely affected thereby.	.	,
The house is further of the opinion that, it these proposals and certain other of the policies of the government are persisted in, as would appear to be the intention of the government as outlined in the speech from the throne, the very serious condition which exists at the^ present time w'ill be intensified rather than relieved.
Last evening a subamendment was moved in this chamber by a representative of the group opposite to my right to strike out of that amendment all the words after the word "That," and to substitute for it a demand for a committee. In other words, the right hon. gentleman has now seen fit to abandon his censorious attitude of the past five weeks. He is no longer condemning the attitude of the government in respect to the Imperial economic conference; he is no longer denouncing the attitude of the government in respect to its policies. Now he says, "I am content now to accept a little amendment that comes from the group in the corner. Per-adventure we will all vote solidly against the government, and all we want is a committee.' That is the spectacle which has been placed before the people of this country. That is the exhibition which has been given. Let the people of Canada know that the Liberal opposition in parliament has no policy and no position, and never had a policy or position except one of destruction. When they find something a little milder than the destruction which they endeavoured to promote and could not secure, they accept it because they say it will let them all vote against the government. That is the position. Is it any wonder that numbers of them hung their heads when they heard the right hon. gentleman say, "I accept this subamendment"?

He did not. I happened to be in London a short time ago, and I know that the leader of the government there was not in his place all the time. He left the house in competent hands, and this house and this government always have been in competent hands when I was absent from the chamber. I was always within the precincts of the chamber; I was only a few feet away discharging duties somewhat more oneroua than listening to the observations made by hon. gentlemen opposite, which would not have been a very difficult task. They know perfectly well that the year before, when they heard the opposition complaining that the Minister of Finance was not in his place when the debate was proceeding but was receiving delegations instead, which the opposi-

The Address-Mr. Bennett
tion of that time thought was taking up too much time, the government of the day said he had to see delegations and to meet people who came to call about public business. I assure this house that I have not been shirking my duties in any sense by not being in this chamber, and now I can see no good, whatever doubt I ever might have entertained, which would have resulted from my being in the chamber, in view of the attitude of the right hon. gentleman that all this discussion has been mere piffle and a waste of time, and that the really important thing is to appoint a committee and waste no further time in these denunciations of policies, economic conferences and so on.
I do stand here to-day to express, as far as it is possible for any member of this house to express, regret that the exaggerated statements^ that have been made with respect to conditions in the west should have been circulated broadcast through this country. I am here to say further that I regret deeply that hon. gentlemen have lent themselves to policies to which, in days gone by, they said they would never be a party. Who does not recall, in 1927, 1928 and 1929, when we ventured to criticize the government, the observations which they then made to the effect that we were injuring the country, that we were pessimists, that we were doing a harm to Canada? Now, broadcast throughout this country and in other countries, have gone statements that cannot be substantiated in any manner or form. It is true that in a few isolated cases you may be able to find hardship; of course you may. There never has been a time when you could not do so, but there are the same people in western Canada to-day as have been there in years gone by. It is the same country; the people have the same high courage and the same determination, except to the extent that the lowering of prices by world conditions, to which I shall presently refer, may have made them less optimistic of the immediate future than they have been in the past.
It ill becomes hon. gentlemen here, who know of an isolated case here and another there, to draw a general conclusion in respect to conditions in western Canada. I can say that in western Canada there are tens of thousands of farmers who have deposits of money in the banks. It is true that there has been great hardship encountered by many farmers, for two reasons, first because of crop failure, and second because of low prices for the crops they did produce. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) himself lost his crop during two succeeding years through no rMr. Bennett.]
fault of his own but through the action of the elements, through drought or hail, and last year, when there was a larger crop, the price for reasons which I shall presently indicate-[DOT] was such as did not leave any profit in return for the labour and money expended.
_ But because you happen to be in opposition is that a good reason to say that you shall at once decry your country? Is it a good reason to say that the people who a few short years ago gave you support are now people who have lost their courage and initiative and power of development? Is that the attitude to take? Is it the right attitude, to say all is lost because you happen to be for the moment defeated? Is it right to take an attitude of pessimism because the people were optimistic and got rid of you? Are those reasons that should govern men in the conduct of the serious business of this country? Then we hear them prattle about cooperation, after they have denounced the country in every way in which they can think, endeavouring to embarrass the administration.
If hon. gentlemen opposite want to know why there has been no declaration of policy during the progress of this debate, they need not do more than look up the rules governing parliamentary practice and procedure. They will find that in Great Britain the speech from the throne is not given precedence over all other business of the house. The business of the house is transacted; bills are introduced; second readings are given; discussions go on, and the ordinary business proceeds, but here we see fit, for reasons best known to ourselves, to give precedence to the address in reply to the speech from the throne over all other business, and in that way we preclude the possibility of measures being introduced or policies declared. Every member of this house who is familiar with parliamentary practice and procedure knows that is so, and in the days of Macdonald and Laurier one day or two days finished the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
