speechtext:
It has been said by one of the foremost authorities on the American continent that the cause of this great depression is speculation-not the narrow speculation to which some hon. gentlemen refer, but speculation in a larger sense. This has brought disaster in its wake. Although the exact figures cannot be ascertained, it is known that over $400,000,000 of Canadian money was lost last year by speculation in Wall street. However, speculation has not been confined to the stock exchanges of New York, Chicago, Montreal and Toronto; it has been spread over every part of this Dominion and of this continent. Think of the speculation in instalment buying, the gambling or staking of one's ability to pay instalments against a wage that might not continue. What is the result? Articles so purchased are taken back by the sellers, which prevents the sale of new articles, thus bringing about overproduction with all its resultant difficulties.
In 1928 I ventured to point out what would happen in Canada by reason of the speculative mania with which the Canadian people were then being attacked. In reply to the Minister of Finance, my words, which appear on page 4044 of Hansard of June 9, 1928, were as follows:
Let him consult the financial heads of great institutions to the south of us. It is true that we have a vast, untouched estate, and that new wealth may be produced much more readily from that than from an old and cultivated estate. But it is also true that where we cultivate, it is necessary that we should sell, and if we find a curtailment and shrinkage of trade among the nations of the world, we find a limitation placed upon our ability to dispose of that which we produce. The minister knows that. He has been told time and time again by the great heads of financial institutions to be cautious, to look ahead. Every thoughtful business man is doing it; everybody is shortening sail except the speculators. Do you realize, sir, that this great speculative era that we now have on the American continent is one fraught with possibilities of the grarmst disaster for this country? The brokers' loans alone in New York last week were over $5,000,000,000, an unheard of figure. In this country speculation is rampant. Some people imagine that trading in pieces of paper upon which there are engraved words and figures constitutes the creation of now wealth. It is not so. The new wealth of the country is being created by the application of labour and capital to the natural resources of the country, and this trading in stock certificates, this great era of speculation in this country and on this continent, is one fraught with possibilities of the gravest danger to Canada, because we have not as they have 111 Sie i n^e(? States a vast accumulation of wealth that will enable us to meet the approaching conditions with ease.
Look at the movement of securities; look at the movement of gold; look at every indication 
there is with respect to speculation in this country. I know great brokers' houses that have declined to take new accounts in this country for over twelve months, one perhaps the greatest brokerage house in this country, because they fear what they see in the distance. But no one in the government seems to care, and if _ we point out the conditions we are pessimists V if we venture to direct attention to the conditions we are ''decrying our coun-tiy . That is the talk that hon. gentlemen opposite hurl at us and before the country. But I recall the language of one who was regarded in t>
-V- years as one of the very greatest of British statesmen, who observed that when their orgy was through, when they had at last recovered from the debauch in which they were then enjoying themselves, possibly then in their sober and quiet moments they would look back and recall the warning that had been given by those who, looking into the future as best they could, guided by those economic signs that were apparent, and by beacon lights, warning of the future, had pointed out the conditions as they also had come to pass. You perhaps will look back upon our warnings, and perhaps remember with at least some degree of fairminded justice the observations that were made bv those of us who have pointed out the national disaster that is inevitable if this orgy of mad expenditure continues.
Those were my words in June, 1928. I pro-fess_ to no special knowledge; I had only the advice that any other hon. member might have had. Anyone who is any student at all of economic conditions, who could not foresee the result, must have been blind to the signs of the times. I know how difficult it is to induce people to realize what is about to happen. Only last week I was looking through certain proceedings in the courts, and I found one brokerage firm $15,000,000 short in a single day. Do hon. members realize what all this means? Did they notice what the courts of Alberta showed as to the number of farmers who had wheat accounts with firms that were before the courts? Have they had the experience I did the other day of a man seventy years of age coming into my office from a remote town in Ontario: he had been well to do, but he went to the little brokerage office in that town, and now he is absolutely without a dollar. That is speculation, and many of the difficulties that confront us in this country to-day arise from that very sort of thing, using the word "speculation" in the large and broad sense in which that term should be employed.
There are some people who try to make it appear that the western country is a country that is bankrupt. I repeat, those gentlemen are entirely wrong. Western Canada is the country it always has been; the people are the people they have ever been. If for a reason that I shall mention, and that I think

it is only fair to mention, the sudden drop in prices, their ardour may have been dampened for a moment, this will not retard them in their advance. It will set them back temporarily, but it will strengthen their courage. But hon. members opposite are not helping to encourage them by decrying their country. They are not doing it by making people abroad believe what they say is true. The other day I had a letter from a gentleman saying: Cannot something be done to stop Mr. So-and-So from talking so about his country? Agreements for sale are being offered abroad, and people overseas say that these have no value because members of parliament say the country is bankrupt. Members of parliament are sometimes accepted as being more important individuals than they are, and their opinion has attached to it an importance that is not warranted. But that is the situation when these things go abroad from Canada's capital city.
How well do I remember in days gone by the present leader of the opposition lecturing me for my pessimism and lack of faith and courage with respect to this Canada of ours, and his saying that to take such an attitude was almost treason to the country. I suggest that hon. gentlemen opposite who, during the last five weeks, have been making the speeches they have, go now and read their leader's observations in days gone by and ask themselves what they think of themselves.
It is true that there was a great diminution in the price of grain. What brought it about? There are hon. gentlemen opposite who scoff and scorn at our mentioning the word ' Russia. Every man knows that the wheat debacle of 1929-30 arose from causes that it is not difficult now to explain but which it might not have then been easy to foresee, although there were many who did foresee them. The world crop of 1929 was known. Some took no account whatever of the Russian crop. The crop of 1930 was known. The price went up beyond one dollar; it went to SI.25 and more, and the farmers of western Canada were told that it would go much higher. They were told that all they had to do was simply to watch and the price would become greater and greater still. I recall farmers who were holding their crops for $2 a bushel, sincerely believing that they were going to get it. They heard of higher prices on the radio; they read of them in the press. What happened? The importing countries, first of all, were increasing their production to a maximum; in the second place, Russia produced a crop of approximately 1,000,000,000 bushels. In other words, Russia had to be reckoned with as an exporting country. I had a friend in the
The Address-Mr. Bennett
grain business go up to Liverpool from London last fall for the purpose of ascertaining just what was involved in this Russian wheat.
He saw wheat which he said was quite the equal of our Canadian wheat of the same grade being sold for sixty cents a bushel, delivered in Liverpool, and the price subsequently went lower. There being an overproduction of wheat, there was a producer willing to sell it at any price he could obtain, a price lower than that of his competitor. Canadian wheat had also to find a lower price level. Practically one-half of that wheat was held by the pools of the country, and unless something were done to steady the financial situation with respect to the pools that held that one-half, then there would be chaos and disaster. This government got behind those pools and said it would assist the orderly marketing of the wheat crop of western Canada. That assistance and support had, of course, the same effect upon non-pool wheat. That was what the government did. It did not peg the price; no government of which I am the head ever will. I have seen artificial prices placed upon commodities and whether that commodity be wheat or anything else, it matters not, I know the inevitable result. It cannot advantageously be done; it will not succeed. It may cause a temporary advantage, but that disappears. Look at the situation in the United States to-day. Mr. Legge, with all his vast experience, with all the millions and hundreds of millions of dollars that he had behind him, declared that the principle of artificial price-fixing was unsound, and it has been abandoned. We did not adopt it, so we did not have to abandon it, but we did give our assistance as I have mentioned.
At this point let me make another observation: some hon. gentlemen have been saying in the house that the attitude taken by Canada at the Imperial conference had the effect of doing what?-lessening the sale of Canadian grain in Great Britain. They thought they would deceive the people of this country by making statements such as that. We have sat in silence while they made those statements, but the time has come to speak, and here are the facts. The total exports to the United Kingdom of wheat in the month of March 1930 were 4,000,000 odd bushels, and in the month of March 1931, 5,000,000 odd bushels. The total exports to the United Kingdom for the eight months of the crop year since August-what think you the figures were?-09,398,672 bushels in 1930, and 96,170,518 in 1931. While the former Minister of Trade and Commerce said that nothing could be done to stimulate or assist the sale of wheat, this government at least
The Address-Mr. Bennett

was doing its level best by every means within its power to stimulate the sale of Canadian grain, not only in the United Kingdom but in other parts of Europe as well, and there is the result in the United Kingdom. Oh, if my hon. friends opposite had only had such a result to talk about, what they would not say 1 But we have sat silent, content to believe that the people of this country wanted action, which they have secured, and not words which they have been receiving during the last five weeks from the benches opposite.
We might have been content with that; but we went to France. France had been buying but little of our wheat. We explained to them the situation and said that if they were to continue receiving the benefits they were receiving under our trade treaty, they must buy larger quantities of our wheat. Listen to the figures. The total of Canadian wheat entering France in January, February and March, 1930, was 1,213,789 bushels. Those were the days of hon. gentlemen opposite. Those were the days when nothing could be done. Here are the figures for the three months after something has been done. For January, February and March, 193ll, the figures were 7,538,860 bushels, and those figures came from the French government themselves, because it frequently happens that cargoes are shipped to France and then deflected to another country after they are afloat, and so we secured these figures from the French government, through Mr. Roy, by cable.

Well, I hope not. I have already said to the right hon. gentleman that there has been a decrease in the values for the reasons I have indicated. Mr. Tardieu, the Premier of France, explained to me that no government could live in France that did not care for the agriculturist; that must be his primary concern. Then he explained what the situation was with respect to wheat. They were growing wheat in their country on every little corner of the soil that could be made available for the purpose, and they put on a duty against foreign wheat which at one time was over $1.50 a bushel, in order that they might stimulate the activities of the domestic growers. When they found that great floods had occurred in the southern parts of France affecting a part of their grain crop, they gave us the benefits which I have indicated, and they have lived up entirely to their obligation and undertaking in that regard. They said they would buy larger {Mr. Bennett.]
quantities from us, and they have done so and will. We think that that is a fairly creditable performance under the circumstances, but we have not blazoned it from the housetops. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that by our attitude abroad we have hurt the market for Canadian wheat. All I can say in reply is this: If as a result of our attitude abroad twelve has become seventy-two, and sixty-nine, ninety-five, let us have more of that attitude.
I have one observation to make with respect to another matter, and that is the agricultural credit corporation in which, while we do not direct it, we have a deep interest. The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to-day released to the press a statement which can be read by all. It just shows how little importance can be attached to the summary kind of statement made in this house by those who either are woefully ignorant or wilfully desire to mislead-one or the other-because a line of inquiry would have elicited the information. But that did not serve the purpose. It sounded well to make an incorrect statement. It might make discontent a little greater, might make people a little more suspicious, might make the unrest a little deeper. That is all that was wanted.
The right hon. gentleman opposite has made some reference to the necessity of action being taken as suggested by the subamendment for the purpose of ensuring that crops would be planted this year. As I have already said, while the amendment was being cogitated over, we were acting. We made an arrangement with the governments of the three western provinces. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) went west, met the representatives of the three prairie governments at Winnipeg, and made arrangements satisfactory to them with respect to the seed grain for the crop of 1931. I wonder if this house realizes that except in 1892, 1916, 1923 and 19-24, the Dominion of Canada has advanced money for seed grain to the prairie provinces from 1876 to 1926. That is not generally known.

The hon. member for Acadia I think was mot endeavouring at the moment to seek from the official leader of the official opposition an interpretation of his very plain language. If that is so, however, we have a much clearer appreciation of what the situation really is. All I can say is that some weeks ago a very definite, clear and sound understanding was arrived at between the provincial governments and ourselves. We did not wait until the time arrived when the crops should be put in; no, we did not wait for that at all. The Minister of Agriculture journeyed to Winnipeg and met the provincial premiers. Having met them an arrangement was made which the premiers thought undesirable to publish to the world. The reasons I think are apparent to everyone. Relief is being given in the manner and form hon. members might expect it to be given, namely by those who know best how it should be given and how the distribution of seed grain should be administered.
Now, sir, I have concluded all I desire to say with respect to this matter. Committees of this house will presently be struck. These committees have power in trade and commerce, in agriculture, in industrial relations, to determine whatever it may be necessary to know in order that we may be able to deal with the situation that lies before us. This government is not in any way, shape or form 22110-50
seeking to escape responsibility. This government seeks no quarter so far as criticism of its actions is concerned. This government realizes that it has come into power at a very, very serious moment in the life of the body politic. It will to the very best of the ability of the members who constitute it discharge its duties as befits Canadians who are trustees for all their fellow citizens. Unswerved from their course by abuse, undeterred by vilification or misrepresentation from any quarter, they will go forward to discharge the duties that the people have placed upon them. If it becomes necessary to ascertain facts, the standing committees of this house are always available. But the government will never palter with its principles in order to retain power. No, if the moment ever comes when the majority of this house conclude it to be desirable that this government should go out, it will go out, but there will be no vacillation, no paltering with the opinions of others to secure support in order that it may continue in power.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to tell my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) how pleased we are that he is back in the house. He has always proved to be a brilliant debater, and I hope that he will help the government to formulate policies that will meet the pressing needs of the people. I like the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) as a man, I admire him as a speaker, but I am sorry that I cannot approve his policies. Like all members to your left, Mr. Speaker, I was expecting a declaration of policy by the head of the government. But what has he given the house? He has given us a lecture on gambling and speculation, that is all. We were treated by the right hon. gentleman as though we were school children. I would remind him that we on this side of the house are full grown men. Sometimes the right hon. gentleman makes gibes about the ignorance and lack of ideas of young members. I think he should acknowledge that we on this side have on several occasions offered him constructive suggestions. For my part, I made a constructive suggestion with reference to the Riviere du Loup station, and on three or four other occasions already this session I have presented constructive suggestions. Apparently the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Fortin) did not understand the purpose of any of those suggestions. Well, I would have been very much surprised if he had understood.
I am in favour, Mr. Speaker, of the subamendment moved by the leader of the Pro-

gressive group (Mr. Gardiner), for the reason that it contains constructive proposals. I am always in favour of such proposals. I do not always agree with what my hon. friends in the far corner say, but whenever they present proposals so constructive in character as those contained in their subamendment I am glad to support them.
The amendment moved by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) contains this clause):

this house, while recognizing the serious economic conditions prevailing throughout the world, regrets that the policies of His Majesty's government have not only failed to afford a remedy for unemployment and agricultural distress, as pledged by the Prime Minister and his colleagues, but have served further to prejudice the deplorable position of the agricultural interests, thereby causing additional unemployment and substantially reducing the national revenue.
That is absolutely true, Mr. Speaker. During the special session last September, a month or two after my right hon. friend had attained power, the number of unemployed in the Dominion was in round figures 100,000; the other day the hon. Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) stated that at the present time the number is 260,000. In other words, under the brief and wonderful administration of my right hon. friend unemployment has increased by 160.000. This, I regret to say, means acute distress for a large number of Canadian families. The amendment continues :
The house believes that the proposals made to the Imperial economic conference and the manner in which they were submitted and discussed by the Prime Minister of Canada were responsible for the failure of the conference to accomplish its purpose in London, and that the successful development of Canada's trade relations with Great Britain has been adversely affected thereby.
With regard to this paragraph, I understand that a very large portion of our surplus wheat still remains unsold. Recently the right hon. Prime Minister characterized a member who had complained of an expenditure of $25 as not being very clever. Apparently a member's ability is to be measured by the magnitude of the figures he deals with, and I suppose that a [DOT] reference to billions and billions of dollars must be taken as the hallmark of cleverness. It may be very interesting to quote substantial figures representing expenditures for gasoline and other commodities, but it must not be forgotten that gasoline is the motive power for tractors, and if people are able to buy gasoline there should be no occasion for them to complain of unemployment. I do not live in the west, but however much the people out there are suffering I

know that the people in my part of the country, especially those engaged in the lumber trade, are very much embarrassed at the present time. The building of skyscrapers in the cities no doubt provides employment, but it affords very little help to the lumber trade, these buildings for the most part being constructed of cement, iron, steel, stone and brick; but in the small country parishes expenditure for lumber enters very very largely into the cost of enlarging their stores or houses or building barns. But for several years while the Liberals were in power the people there listened to the blue ruin talk of hon. members opposite. At that time -conditions were very much better than they are now; was it in order to gain power that my hon. friends were so pessimistic about the future of this county? Because of the pessimism preached by hon. gentlemen opposite many -people living in the country did not spend money for lumber in order to carry on construction. They said to themselves, "The leader of the Conservative party is a great financier and business man, and he must know something about the future of this country. It will be better if we save our money."

Hon. gentlemen opposite, as they themselves fully realize are responsible for that situation, and the consequences have been very serious. The lumber remains in the yards unsold; there are no more shanties in the woods in the winter, and the carpenters and workmen of the small parishes go to the cities because they cannot find employment in their own villages. This is what has happened, and hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible.
I heard the Prime Minister say, "I have never said anything to hurt the future of this country", and he read what he had said last June in answer to the Minister of Finance of that time. It is all very well to say that conditions throughout the country are good, but the other day in that Tory paper, the Montreal Gazette, i-t was -pointed out that within the last few months there had been a slump in trade amounting to some $600,000,000.

I should like to say a word about the banks. I believe our banking system is very good, but often the bank clerks and employees are insufficiently paid. That is a shame; there are young men in the banks who handle thousands of dollars every day and who are not paid a wage commensurate with the importance or responsibility of their services. The Minister of Finance should confer with the heads of the banker's association to see if those salaries cannot be increased.
During the last campaign the government told the people, in my contituency at least, that the Mackenzie King government was doing too much for the west. This statement was made repeatedly in my county by Tory speakers; they said the Liberal government was tied up with the west in political matters and that the east was suffering therefrom.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we on this side of the house are proud to support our leader. We are ready also to give full support to proper government measures if the Prime Minister will do something more than lecture the hon. members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, before this vote is proceeded with, contrary to my habit and very much contrary to my inclination, I desire to take part for a second time in this debate. Owing to some statements that have been made and owing to the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) I feel it incumbent upon me to offer a few comments and to make a brief statement. I may remind the house that the amendment having been disposed of, it is fully in accord with the rules that I should now speak to the main motion.
I think I can characterize some of the statements made by the Prime Minister in respect of this corner of the house as being in the first place rather unjustifiable and in respect of a part of his attitude at least,
almost one might say deliberately or gratuitously offensive to some of the members here. I am not now making any comment upon the utterances of the Prime Minister as addressed to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), I am taking no part, and I intend to take no part, in any exchange of political animosities. However,
I may remind the house that during the entire debate every hon. member in this corner of the chamber who spoke refrained most assiduously and most meticulously from making any statement of a condemnatory character. They have refrained from taking an attitude of partisanship. They have outlined conditions as they knew them to exist; they have offered certain suggestions, as they thought, tending towards their amelioration, and to-day-I am sorry to say it-when at last the Prime Minister takes part in the debate he throws back in our faces our offer of friendly cooperation. He repudiates the assistance we sought to give in meeting the conditions which prevail, and he characterizes our statements as exaggerated, as being not according to facts, as tending not towards the betterment but towards the imperilling of the future of this country. He characterizes our statements in regard to conditions with which we are absolutely familiar as not only exaggerated but as carrying weight throughout this country and throughout the world only in virtue of the position which we occupy and not by virtue of either the common sense, the knowledge or I might say the accuracy of statement on the part of the members themselves.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wonder just what solace it will bring to the hearts of men and women at home who, whatever the Prime Minister may say, are looking to this parliament for help. They are suffering, and I wonder what comfort it will bring them to have it stated that except in those districts in western Canada where for years there have -been crop failures, there is no farmer who has not been guilty of wild speculation in the widest sense but is to-day comfortable and prosperous and happy.

I did understand the Prime Minister to say that except for the results of speculation, using the word in the widest sense, farmers who had not suffered from repeated crop failures were, as a class, in prosperous and happy circumstances. I think I am doing no injustice to the Prime Minister when I say that, because I think I am using almost his exact words.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to bring forward any individual cases. I agree with the right hon. Prime Minister in that one may bring individual cases which are exceptions to the rule and which may prove anything. One may bring individual cases of intense hardship in times of wide prosperity. One may bring individual cases of comparative affluence in times of general penury, and these cases will prove nothing. I do say, however, from the intimate knowledge which I possess of that part of Alberta in which I have resided for forty years, that as a general rule and taking the great majority of the citizens there, they are not in a position either of comfort, of happiness or of affluence, nor have any great percentage of them been guilty of speculation even in the widest sense of the term. They are men who have been working and are working to-day, men who have done their best, but owing to the conditions which we know exist, conditions in relation to low prices, which have not returned the cost of production during the last year or two, they find themselves at the moment without the necessary funds with which to carry on their farming operations.
May I say this further, Mr. Speaker, that when I listened to the Prime Minister, in reference to the enormous wealth which has been created in those provinces during the last three years, I wondered if they were the same three provinces which I heard described not so many months ago as being in a state of distress owing to the misgovernment of the ten years preceding. Conditions have not changed since then except for the worse- not because of any fault of the government, but rather because of the operation of natural forces and the continual lowering of prices.
I have stated and re-stated the facts which I know to be true. I have expressed the disappointment-I shall not say the regret- which I felt at the refusal of the offer made in good part by hon. members in this house of cooperation and assistance rather than a threat of partisan warfare. We regret that, because we had intended so to conduct ourselves in the house during this session that 
we would have demonstrated the fact that we place the welfare of the country above party warfare, and we had hoped that that would be the attitude adopted at least for this session. If that is not to be the attitude adopted, it seems to me that little hope is offered. If we are to be told that no need exists, then in the opinion of the government no policy is necessary to relieve that distress, and, that being the case, how can I look upon the speech from the throne? It has become what I refused to call it five weeks ago, a hollow, watery grave. I voted against the amendment because I believed that it offered nothing of value to my people or to Canada, and I must stand in my place and vote against the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne because I feel no gratitude or can see no hope as I read its terms or as I listen to the speeches delivered thereon.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention again to address the house on the subject matter now under discussion, but I feel it my duty to do so because of the statements made this afternoon by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). One has only to go back twelve months or so to the time when the present Prime Minister was the leader of the opposition and when those now supporting him were in opposition to the then Liberal government to recall the debates staged on going into supply .for the purpose of trying to make the government of the day take cognizance of the distress then prevailing in many parts of Canada. It is a curious thing that the conditions which existed while a party was in opposition suddenly and for some unaccountable reason, change when they come into office and assume the responsibility of government.
When speaking this afternoon the Prime Minister directed some of his remarks to this corner of the house. He said: The exaggerated statements of -conditions in the west are not true in any way, shape or form. I do not know where the Prime Minister obtains his information, unless it be from the secretary of the Canadian Bankers' Association. If he believes that such information is absolutely correct then I can understand the position he adopted this afternoon. I say without fear of contradiction that those who have recently had the opportunity of visiting the west and meeting the people actually living on the land ought to know more about conditions than those who have not had such an opportunity. It is unfortunate that important or so-called important persons from eastern Can-

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
ada seem to obtain their information with regard to conditions in western Canada from such places as the lobby of the Palliser hotel in Calgary. They do not seem to be given the opportunity of getting out among the people and finding out just how they are being affected by present conditions. Under these circumstances perhaps they may be excused if they make certain rash statements, because they probably believe that the information which they have obtained is correct.
I made a statement yesterday which I intend to discuss for a moment or two. It was as follows:
May I say also. Mr. Speaker, that in my judgment if the farmers of western Canada to-day were forced to liquidate, eighty per cent of them would be insolvent, notwithstanding all that has been said by my good friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins).
I sincerely believed that statement to be true, but further on in my remarks I made this reservation:
If price levels get better they may be able to get away from that condition but, sir, if this condition continues for another twelve months my advice to the western farmer will be that his only hope is to go through bankruptcy.
I made that statement in all sincerity and I do not appreciate the Prime Minister questioning my veracity.
The Prime Minister called the attention of the house this afternoon to the tremendous volume of wealth produced by the western farmer. He quoted figures to the effect that during the last three years there had been produced new wealth to the tune of $1,900,000,000. and that new mineral wealth had been produced to the extent of $100,000,000, or a total of $2,000,000,000. He asked the question: Where has all this wealth gone to? May I say that as far as the farmer is concerned, the man who really produced this wealth, it did not go into the purchase of expensive automobiles. In my opinion there is no person in Canada more entitled to an automobile than the man living on a farm, ten, twenty, thirty or forty miles away from a town. I know something about what an automobile means to a man on a farm, and I say this, if I were to farm some distance from town and could not afford an old tin Lizzie of some description, I would not farm very long. An automobile has become one of the necessities of farm life. The farmer appreciates the convenience it offers, and in view of the fact that he is the producer of new wealth I say that it ill behooves the Prime Minister to point to the farmer as having squandered his wealth on the purchase of automobiles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I did not at any time say that he had squandered his wealth. I did not even suggest that. I merely said that men possessing $300,000,000 worth of cars were not poor.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I accept the Prime Minister's correction, and I gladly take back the words which I used in that regard.
The Prime Minister, I believe, also made the statement, not this afternoon but when he was speaking earlier in the session, that he wondered why the western farmer, after having produced so much wealth, did not save. If the Prime Minister had an opportunity of going out to that western country and homesteading, opening up a new farm and going through all the trials and troubles which that entails: if he had had that experience, I am satisfied he never would have asked such a foolish question. It is only about twenty-five years since the opening up of western Canada began. Prior to that time we had a fringe of settlement along the main line of the Canadian Pacific, along the line from Regina to Prince Albert and also along the line from Calgary to Edmonton, so that the west is practically a new country. Indeed, it is being developed every day.
What is the position of the man who goes on new land in western Canada? He has the hope that he is going to make a home for himself and his family. It is true that we had a few speculators, but the primary hope of the person who goes on a homestead or takes up new land in the west is to create a home for himself and his family. During the first few years they are on those farms, they do not spend much money. I know how some of those people have lived in order to develop the property which they had under their control at that particular time. I know the aspirations of those people; I know the moment they made any money on those new farms they put it back into new developments, such as breaking up more land, clearing bush, fencing, or adding to their homes or barns or granaries as the case might be. Why? Because the only money they had to develop the property was what they earned from it. That is the spirit of the west. We are not yet old enough in the west to have accumulated great wealth. Therefore when the farmers of the west have a good year, if after having met their liabilities in full or in part, they have any money left, that money is reinvested in their property for the purpose of further developing it. If that had not been so, western Canada would not have been half as well de-

Thank you. He stated
that most of those people to-day were being fed by the country or by charitable organizations. So far as immigration is concerned, I think that the immigration policy of this country for the last few years has been rotten. I use that term because of the fact that immigration has brought upon this country a greater burden than we should have had to carry. But I do not think that the Prime Minister should try to get away from the responsibility that properly falls upon his shoulders because of the fact that very many members of his own party were continually calling for more and more immigration.
The only other point with which I wish to deal is with regard to the assistance which the government has given to western Canada. It is quite true that this government has devised a policy, and I congratulate them upon it, for assistance in the way of seed,
feed and so forth. I think that the government has done very well in that regard. But may I point out to the Prime Minister this great weakness in that proposal. In order to secure seed relief or feed, and so forth, it is necessary for the individual to make an application to the municipal council, and I know that many municipal councils feel that because of the unpaid taxes due to their municipalities and the obligations which are now upon them they are not justified in even risking being called upon to pay 25 per cent of any ultimate loss that may occur. Consequently, under these circumstances, I believe that many of the farmers of the west will be denied the seed and feed that they require; but of course that probably is not the fault of the present government.

speechtext:
I quite appreciate that. I said 25 per cent of the ultimate losses. The great problem at the present time, however, is not so much the question of seed and feed. The great problem to-day is bank credit. The farmers require credit to-day more than feed and seed to put a crop in. I know that from actual experience. If you do not happen to be one of the fortunate ones possessing a bank account, it is necessary to go to the bank and secure a loan. That is the greatest immediate problem that I see before western Canada, and my judgment is this:	If the
people of Canada think that the western wheat crop is of any great value to this country, then it will be necessary for the government to take action along whatever lines they deem expedient to see that reason-, able credit is afforded to those who put in crops. That is very important, and it should be done immediately, otherwise it will be of no value.
The Prime Minister this afternoon, in twitting the right hon. leader of the opposition in regard to markets for wheat, pointed with pride to the greater amount of wheat which had been exported by Canada during the last eight months as compared with the previous eight months, and took credit to his government for being able to assist the grain trade and the pools in selling that wheat. But does the house realize that every bushel of wheat ' shipped out of this country means a dead loss of from 30 to 40 cents a bushel? Yet the Prime Minister prides himself on the attitude which his government has taken in assisting to send wheat out of this country-

The Address-Miss Macphail
at a loss of from 30 to 40 cents a bushel. It is always easier to sell a larger amount of wheat when it is cheap, particularly when the price falls below the cost of production, than to sell it at the cost of production or at cost plus a profit.

I wish I knew. If my hon. friend could tell me that, he and I might be able to make a little money on the side.
I merely wish to say in closing that I take exception to some of the remarks made by the Prime Minister this afternoon. I believe that they were unwarranted by the actual conditions such as we know them to exist in western Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I listened with amazement to the
Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) speaking this afternoon. I wondered could it be just one year ago that we heard the unemployment debate in this house, a debate in which the government of that day showed a complete lack of understanding of conditions in the country. At that time the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister was the leader of the opposition, and he and his colleagues told the house, and in many instances told very well, what the conditions were. Then we went through an election last July. We heard the moaning of the then opposition from coast to coast. The conditions were terrible. They were such that only God's anointed could save the country. There is no use in the Prime Minister now getting up as he did to-day and assuming the air of lecturing this house, particularly this corner of the house. I think the Prime Minister will find as time goes on that the speech which he made this afternoon was an exceedingly unwise one, and one which he will bitterly regret.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He may not-he ought. The conditions since the unemployment debate last session and since the election held in July last year have not improved. On the contrary they have steadily become worse. Had the Prime Minister risen in his place to-day in the house and admitted that such was the case and that present conditions required the best efforts of every hon. member of the house he would have won the hearts of hon. members, because even this house has a heart. However he did not do that; he would not admit that serious conditions pre-

vail, conditions with which all working people are familiar. It might do the Prime Minister some good if he went out and became acquainted with the facts. I think it is most unfortunate and ridiculous that the Prime Minister has not seen fit to admit the present condition in Canada. I would think that during the next two or three weeks editorials in our newspapers would make the blunder abundantly clear, even to the ministry who now grace the treasury benches.
During the Easter vacation I happened to be out west. During my visit I had occasion to speak with an alderman of the city of Regina, and he told me that he had attended a council meeting and a meeting of the relief committee which had been working all winter. They were very desirous of closing up their relief measures but they still had 2,300 married men who were without relief or employment. He said the difficulty was that the men were determined not to work for $10 or $15 a month, and that that was all the farmers surrounding the city of Regina were in a position to pay. This gentleman was in a position to view both sides of the question, both from the standpoint of the unemployed and that of the farmer. He said that under the circumstances the farmers could not pay the high wages they had paid in former years. In the spring of the year it is expected that unemployment should ease up. The unemployed men are absorbed in the new spring work on the farms. I was not surprised to read in the newspapers about the riot in Winnipeg. When I was in that city walking along Portage avenue and Main street I saw badly dressed men with nothing to do, just milling around, moving up and down. They were going nowhere, they were not walking fast, but just killing time. They walked one way and then the other. By law they are required to keep moving and that is the way they did it. I am not blaming the Prime Minister for the unemployment and stress, but I am blaming him for not admitting that such a condition exists. Why does he not admit that there are such conditions? It is true that the farmers are not unemployed; they are unpaid. They have plenty of work to do. There has been talk about new wealth which was created in western Canada. Where did it go? It went to provide profits to the people who benefited from the tariff. It went to provide bankers with their large dividends. Hon. members laugh! It may sound amusing, but it really is not a matter to be treated lightly. The wealth of western Canada has gone to provide bankers with dividends, to build fine

office buildings such as we see in the cities of Toronto, Montreal, Regina and Calgary. It has gone to provide a better living for other classes in Canada. When the farmer had paid out all these profits he had nothing left for himself.
For a moment or two I want to touch on the subject of immigration. This afternoon I directed a question to the Prime Minister when he was intimating-I hope I am quoting
him correctly-

-intimating that the excessive immigration into this country was the fault of the Liberal government. May I say to him that the Liberals have enough to bear without alone carrying that responsibility. I can recall, as can the veterans of this house, that for ten years the hon. members in this corner of the house have said, and never more clearly than in the year 19212, that it was a very foolish policy constantly to bring in immigrants to this country. Let me quote from a speech by the present Prime Minister delivered in the House of Commons on Monday, February 11. 1929. At that time he was making comment on the speech from the throne and complaining there was not enough money spent on immigration. He said:
' We have here one of the largest undeveloped areas of the world; we have a very pressing necessity for more people. There need be no misapprehension about that, notwithstanding what has been said from time to time to the contrary. It will be found that the increase of population in this country, brought about through bringing additional people in, will not only lessen unemployment for those who are now in it, but will increase all employment.
The quotation is much longer, but that is sufficient.

members opposite did not take the same attitude ten years ago, and the Liberal government also.
